title: Guillain–Barre syndrome after myocardial infarction: a case report and literature review
case_prompt:
A 75-year-old Chinese woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, atrial fibrillation, and prior cerebral infarction experienced sudden loss of consciousness while eating. After sublingual nitroglycerin, her consciousness returned but chest tightness persisted. An electrocardiogram showed ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, aVF, V3R–V5R, V7–V9, reciprocal ST depression in I and aVL, and a IIIA-V block, indicating inferior, anterior, posterior, and right-ventricular MI. Coronary angiography revealed 90% stenosis of the proximal left anterior descending artery, occlusion of the distal posterior left ventricular branch, and diffuse 85% stenosis in the mid right coronary artery with thrombus autolysis. She underwent emergency PCI of the mid right coronary artery.

Twenty hours before transfer, she noted subacute bilateral upper-limb weakness (MRC sum score 54), progressing distally to proximally with numbness, followed by similar bilateral lower-limb weakness and urinary retention. Cranial CT was unremarkable.

On ICU transfer, she was afebrile, blood pressure 169/97 mmHg, ventricular rate 105 bpm (atrial fibrillation). Exam showed hypotonia of all four limbs, complete quadriplegia, superficial hypoesthesia in the extremities, dysarthria, decreased pharyngeal reflex, absent cough reflex, and tendon areflexia. Cerebellar and funduscopic exams and other cranial nerves were normal.

CBC, blood smear, C-reactive protein, electrolytes, liver and renal function tests were normal. Serum total protein 6.5 g/dL, albumin 3.039 g/dL, globulin 3.5 g/dL. Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM, EBV capsid antigen–IgM, EBV nuclear antigen–IgM, CMV IgM, CMV pp65 antigen, and HIV antibodies were negative. BNP was 526.44 pg/mL (normal 0–100), procalcitonin 1.69 ng/mL (normal <0.05). Family refused lumbar puncture. Due to her critical condition, nerve conduction studies and electromyography could not be performed.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Critical illness polyneuropathy often occurs in multi-organ failure or sepsis, which was not present initially — “They often occur in clinical conditions with multi-organ failure and sepsis…”  
2. Critical illness myopathy is linked to prolonged high-dose neuromuscular blockers or steroids, neither of which the patient had received — “after the long-term use of large doses of neuromuscular blockers and steroids…”  
3. Critical illness neuromyopathy presents with limb and respiratory weakness but requires severe ICU insults absent here — “They often manifest as limb weakness, palsy, and respiratory muscle weakness…”  
4. Acute quadriplegic myopathy also arises in multi-organ failure or sepsis, which did not precede her weakness — “They often occur in clinical conditions with multi-organ failure and sepsis…”  
5. Guillain–Barre syndrome presents with acute flaccid paralysis, areflexia, bulbar and respiratory involvement matching this patient’s exam — “The clinical diagnosis of GBS was based on clinical symptoms, including acute tetraplegia, bulbar weakness, and respiratory failure with areflexia.”  
6. Multiple antiganglioside antibodies strongly support GBS in the absence of CSF or NCS confirmation — “Presence of serum anti-GT1a IgG antibodies, anti-GM1 IgG antibodies, and anti-GM2 IgG antibodies favoured the diagnosis of GBS.”
